title: Campus canteen pre-ordering at lunch rush

authoring.author: Parikshaa content team
authoring.originality: Written for Parikshaa: our own canteen pre-order design case, examples, code, quiz and explanations; no text from any site, book or course.

scenario: A university with **40,000 students** and 12 canteens wants an app where students order lunch before class ends, pay by UPI, and pick it up at a chosen 10-minute slot without queueing. Popular items (veg biryani on Fridays) run out, and each canteen's kitchen can make only so many plates per slot. Design the backend.

clarifying_questions.a: About 25,000 orders a day, 70% of them between 12:30 and 13:30.
Stock per item per day (e.g. 300 biryani plates) and kitchen capacity per 10-minute slot (e.g. 60 plates).
UPI through a payment gateway; the gateway confirms by a callback a few seconds later, sometimes twice.

clarifying_questions.q: What if payment fails or the student never pays?
clarifying_questions.a: The reserved plate must go back to stock within a few minutes.
Yes: a kitchen screen lists orders per slot, and a pickup screen marks orders collected.
One campus, one cloud region; multi-region is out of scope.

functional: Browse menus with live availability per canteen
Place an order for a pickup slot, holding stock and slot capacity
Pay by UPI; confirm the order only after payment
Release holds when payment fails or times out
Kitchen and pickup screens per canteen

non_functional.name: Peak orders
non_functional.target: about 10 orders per second sustained at lunch, bursts of 50

non_functional.name: Correctness
non_functional.target: never sell more plates or slot capacity than exist

non_functional.name: Latency
non_functional.target: p99 under 500 ms to place an order (excluding UPI)

estimates.question: Average order rate during the lunch hour if 70% of 25,000 daily orders fall in that hour?
estimates.working: 25,000 × 0.7 = 17,500 orders in 3,600 s ≈ 4.9 per second; bursts (class ends at the same minute) are about 10 times that.

estimates.question: Menu reads per second at lunch if each ordering student opens menus 8 times and half of the 40,000 students order on a given day?
estimates.working: 20,000 students × 8 reads = 1,60,000 reads, mostly in the same hour: 1,60,000 / 3,600 ≈ 44 per second.

estimates.question: Storage for one year of orders at 1 KB per order (with items and status history), in GB?
estimates.working: 25,000 × 365 × 1 KB ≈ 91,25,000 KB ≈ 9.1 GB a year: a single relational database is plenty.

expected_components.name: Order service with a relational database
expected_components.why: Orders, holds and payments need transactions so stock and slot counts never go below zero.

expected_components.name: Inventory and slot counters updated atomically
expected_components.why: A conditional update (stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0) makes overselling impossible even with concurrent orders.

expected_components.name: Hold with expiry (reservation)
expected_components.why: Stock is held while the student pays and released if payment does not complete in time.

expected_components.name: Payment gateway integration with idempotent callbacks
expected_components.why: UPI callbacks can arrive twice or late; the order must be confirmed exactly once.

expected_components.name: Menu read cache
expected_components.why: Menus are read far more than they change; cache them for a few seconds and show availability as approximate.

expected_components.name: Expiry worker or delayed queue
expected_components.why: Releases holds whose payment window has passed.

expected_components.name: Push channel to kitchen and pickup screens
expected_components.why: Screens update as orders are confirmed and collected, without polling the database.

expected_components.name: Notification service
expected_components.why: Tells the student when the order is ready.

api: GET /canteens/{id}/menu → items with price and approximate availability
POST /orders {canteen, slot, items[], idempotency_key} → order in state HELD with a payment link
data_model: items(canteen_id, item_id, name, price, stock_today); slots(canteen_id, slot_start, capacity, used); orders(order_id, student_id, canteen_id, slot_start, state HELD|PAID|CANCELLED|COLLECTED, hold_expires_at, idempotency_key UNIQUE); order_lines(order_id, item_id, qty); payments(txn_id UNIQUE, order_id, status, received_at).

diagram.alt: The student app talks to an API gateway; menu reads go to a cache in front of the database; orders go to the order service, which updates stock and slots in the database and calls the payment gateway; payment callbacks return to the order service; an expiry worker releases old holds; kitchen screens get updates over a push channel.

data.source:
flowchart LR
  App[Student app] --> GW[API gateway]
  GW -->|menus| MC[(Menu cache)]
  MC --> DB[(Orders DB)]
  GW -->|orders| OS[Order service]
  OS --> DB
  OS -->|payment link| PG[UPI gateway]
  PG -->|callback| OS
  EW[Expiry worker] --> DB
  OS --> PUSH[Push channel]
  PUSH --> KS[Kitchen screens]

deep_dives.body: Placing an order runs one transaction: decrement each item's stock with `UPDATE items SET stock_today = stock_today - :qty WHERE item_id = :id AND stock_today >= :qty`, increment the slot with `UPDATE slots SET used = used + :plates WHERE ... AND used + :plates <= capacity`, and insert the order as HELD with `hold_expires_at = now + 5 min`. If any update touches zero rows, roll back and tell the student what ran out. Because each check-and-change is one statement, two students can never both take the last plate.

deep_dives.topic: Payments that arrive twice, late or never
deep_dives.body: The callback handler looks up the order and moves it HELD → PAID only if it is still HELD, in the same transaction that records `txn_id` (unique). A second callback finds the txn_id already stored and returns 200 without changes. If the callback arrives after the hold expired and stock was released, we try to re-take the stock; if it is gone, we refund automatically. The expiry worker moves HELD orders past `hold_expires_at` to CANCELLED and gives their stock and slot back, in one transaction.

Menu reads are ten times order writes. Serving them from a short-lived cache (5-10 seconds) keeps the database free for orders. Availability on the menu is therefore approximate; the order transaction is the real check, and the app explains politely when an item sold out between viewing and ordering.

trade_offs: A relational database with conditional updates is simpler and safer than a distributed counter at 10 orders per second; it would be revisited only at far higher scale.
Holding stock during payment can briefly show items as sold out that later return; a short hold window limits it.
Cached menus can be a few seconds stale; correctness is enforced at order time instead.
failure_modes: The payment gateway is slow: holds expire and stock returns; late successes are re-checked or refunded.
The expiry worker stops: holds pile up and items look sold out; alert on the count of expired-but-held orders.
The database is down: ordering stops; menus may still be served from cache with an 'ordering paused' banner.

rubric.criterion: Clarifies limits (stock, slot capacity), payment behaviour and peak hours.
Estimates order rate, read rate and storage, and concludes one database suffices.
Prevents overselling with atomic conditional updates or equivalent locking.
Designs holds with expiry and idempotent payment confirmation, including late and duplicate callbacks.
Separates heavy menu reads (cache) from order writes.
Explains trade-offs and failure handling clearly (AI feedback, advice only).

concept_checks.stem: Two students order the last biryani at the same moment. What guarantees only one succeeds?
options: UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock >= 1, checking rows affected
concept_checks.explanation: Check and change in one atomic statement; zero rows affected means sold out.

concept_checks.stem: The UPI gateway sends the same success callback twice. What makes this safe?
options: A unique txn_id and moving the order HELD → PAID only if it is still HELD
concept_checks.explanation: Idempotent handling: the second callback finds the transaction already recorded.

concept_checks.stem: Why hold stock before payment completes?
options: So a student who is paying cannot lose the plate to someone else, while unpaid holds expire
concept_checks.explanation: The hold reserves the plate for a short, bounded time.

concept_checks.stem: At about 5 orders per second, what is the simplest correct store for orders and stock?
concept_checks.explanation: The load is small; transactions give correctness simply.

revision_card.front: Pre-order with limited stock and payment in between: the three mechanisms?
revision_card.back: Atomic conditional updates (stock - n WHERE stock >= n) so nothing is oversold; a hold with expiry released by a worker; idempotent payment callbacks (unique txn_id, HELD → PAID only once).
